title: Kuperberg's algorithm and CSIDH
one_liner: Commutativity buys CSIDH its small keys and non-interactive key exchange, and costs it a subexponential quantum attack — whose concrete cost is still disputed.
description: Why the CSIDH class-group action is an abelian hidden shift problem, how Kuperberg's subexponential quantum algorithm applies, and what the parameter dispute between the Peikert and CSIDH camps actually turns on.
standfirst: CSIDH was not broken. It was repriced, repeatedly, by analyses that disagree about what a quantum computer costs to run — and the disagreement is a more instructive object than either answer, because it is about cost models rather than about mathematics.

facts.Classical cost: Õ(√|cl(O)|) ≈ p<sup>1/4</sup>, by meet-in-the-middle or random walk
facts.Status: Unbroken; parameter sizes contested, CSIDH-512 widely considered insufficient
facts.Not affected by: The SIDH torsion attacks — no torsion images are published

blocks.p: CSIDH, introduced by Castryck, Lange, Martindale, Panny and Renes, works with supersingular elliptic curves defined over Fp rather than over Fp2. Restricting to the prime field makes the endomorphism ring commutative — an order O in an imaginary quadratic field — and its ideal class group then acts on the set of such curves, freely and transitively:

blocks.label: A free, transitive group action — a torsor, not a group

blocks.p: That action commutes, so key exchange is the obvious thing: Alice publishes [a]·E0, Bob publishes [b]·E0, and both compute [a][b]·E0. Nothing else is transmitted — and that absence is why CSIDH survived the attacks that ended SIDH. The prize is real: very small public keys, and genuine non-interactive key exchange, which no lattice-based KEM provides.
The price is the same commutativity. A group action whose group is abelian is precisely the setting of the abelian hidden shift problem, and that problem has a subexponential quantum algorithm.

Recovering Alice's secret from [a]·E0 means inverting the group action. Define two functions on the group, one built from E0 and one from [a]·E0; they are equal up to a shift by the unknown [a]. Finding that shift is the abelian hidden shift problem, and Kuperberg gave a quantum sieve for it running in

blocks.math: 2<sup>O(√(log N))</sup> quantum queries and time, for a group of order N
blocks.label: Subexponential — between Grover's √N and Shor's polynomial time

blocks.p: The sieve prepares many phase-encoded states over the group and combines them pairwise, each combination concentrating the unknown shift into fewer, more useful bits, until the shift can be read out. Regev gave a variant using polynomial quantum space at somewhat greater time; Kuperberg's second algorithm improved the tradeoff again. The important structural point is what the algorithm is not: it is not Shor. Commutativity is enough for a subexponential quantum attack and not enough for a polynomial-time one, which is exactly the narrow ledge CSIDH stands on.

Classically the picture is unremarkable. Inverting the action is a search over the class group, done by meet-in-the-middle or a random-walk collision search in Õ(√|cl(O)|), which for CSIDH parameters is about p1/4. Classical security therefore scales the way generic attacks always do.

The exponent is agreed. What is contested is the constant, the query count, and above all what a quantum query costs — and at subexponential asymptotics those decide everything at real parameter sizes.

ul: The original proposal offered CSIDH-512 as a NIST level 1 parameter set, on an analysis of Kuperberg-style attacks available at the time.

Peikert gave a concrete analysis of the collimation sieve applied to CSIDH and concluded that CSIDH-512 falls well short of that claim — that the quantum work is far smaller than the proposers had estimated.
Bonnetain and Schrottenloher reached similarly reduced security estimates by a different route.

Bernstein, Lange, Martindale and Panny costed the quantum circuits for evaluating the group action in detail, arguing that the per-query cost of a real implementation is high enough to change the conclusion substantially.
Chávez-Saab, Chi-Domínguez, Jaques and Rodríguez-Henríquez took the conservative branch and showed that much larger parameters — CSIDH-4096 and beyond — remain implementable, if slower.

blocks.p: The disagreement is not about the mathematics. It is about the cost model: whether quantum random access memory is free or expensive, whether an attack is allowed unbounded circuit depth or must fit within a realistic time limit, and how much error-correction overhead a long-running quantum computation carries. Different defensible answers to those questions produce security estimates that differ by tens of bits.

blocks.note: A quantum security claim is a claim about a cost model, and it is worth no more than the model it names. When someone quotes a post-quantum security level, the first question is which model produced it — depth-limited or not, QRAM free or costed. Two papers can be simultaneously correct and 40 bits apart.

blocks.p: The practical consequence today is a consensus that CSIDH-512 is not a level 1 parameter set, and disagreement about exactly how much larger is enough. CSIDH is not a NIST candidate and is not deployed at scale; it remains an active research object, valued for the non-interactive key exchange that nothing else in the post-quantum portfolio offers.
Kuperberg's algorithm needs the group to be abelian. That single hypothesis partitions the isogeny landscape cleanly:

ul: CSIDH and CSI-FiSh use a commutative class-group action, so the attack applies and sets their quantum parameters.
SIDH and SIKE used the non-commutative supersingular graph over Fp2, so Kuperberg never applied to them — they fell to something else entirely, the torsion-point attacks.
SQIsign is likewise non-commutative, resting on the endomorphism-ring problem via the Deuring correspondence. Kuperberg does not reach it.

The general supersingular isogeny path problem has no known subexponential quantum attack; claw-finding approaches give about p1/3 quantum against √p classical, with severe memory costs that argue against the quantum advantage being real.

blocks.p: Read the two isogeny pages in this library together and the trade is explicit. SIDH published extra data to make its non-commutative walk usable, and the extra data is what killed it. CSIDH needs no extra data because commutativity does that work — and commutativity is what exposes it to Kuperberg. Each scheme paid for its key exchange in a different currency, and the community found out what each price was, in one case abruptly and in the other by a decade of argument that is still running.
